Talk outline: sampling design for spatial cluster randomized trials with spillover

Draft 3 (2026-10-28). The deck is built (spillover_talk.qmd), and the slide entries below are generated from it by tools/outline_from_deck.py, so they always describe the deck as rendered. Edit the deck, re-render, then regenerate this file and outline.html. Everything above the marker line is written by hand.

The deck serves two talks: Part I of the prelim (Monday 2026-12-07; about 20 minutes per part; committee of four statisticians and Dr. Van Deinse) and Dr. Lin's conference talk in December (statisticians). Tags: both (same slide in both talks), prelim (prelim only), conference (standalone or conference only; the prelim drops it). Prelim and conference notes say how a slide changes.

Decisions (author, 2026-10-28)

  • The corrected 3×3 and 3×4 results are simply the results. The slides never mention the correction, and there is no correction backup slide or status line.
  • Framing: BSS is a good design, not the best or the worst, against rolling the dice on one SRS allocation. The results lead with where BSS falls among the random allocations, and the deck says plainly that most random allocations beat BSS when spillover reaches both arms (checkerboard collinearity). Per-scenario "optimal allocation" counts are left out. "Checkerboard paradox" is not used.
  • The BSS-rank percentages appear on slides only; Chapter 2 is not changed.
  • The 3×3 and 3×4 grids get one main slide (both grids side by side); their full figures and tables are in backup.
  • Background carries the prelim's shared motivation (trials of places, spillover, spatial dependence) and Part I's own prior work and gap (analysis-stage methods vs design-stage options, from the literature review). No standalone literature review.
  • Notation is Part I's own (β intervention effect, ψ spillover, ρ spatial dependence, cluster-level outcome). Part II defines its own; no harmonizing, no bridge slide.
  • The results are presented as published. What ρ = 0.01 means on the fitted scale (about 0.5) is explained in a backup slide; see ../review/notes/2026-10-28-rho-scale-note.md.
  • The paper reference is on the last Discussion slide. The standalone deck ends with a thank-you slide (Dr. Lin, Dr. Van Deinse; NIMH K01MH129619 and BJA 15PBJA-24-GG-01896-PRJH). In the prelim these acknowledgements move to the single closing slide after Part III.
  • Every number on the slides and in the script is computed at render time from results/ and review/ (tools/load_results.R), not typed by hand.

Shorter conference slots

The conference slot is not known yet; the deck assumes about 20 minutes.

  • 15–20 minutes: merge "NC MCO areas" into "NC probation districts", and say the neighbor definition in one sentence instead of showing "Neighbors". Saves about 1.25 minutes.
  • 10–15 minutes: also cut "Trials of places" (one sentence on "Spillover"), fold "Spatial dependence" into "Spillover", reduce "The design gap" to its bottom card, and cut "Control & intervention clusters" and "Larger grids" (one sentence each on "Choosing a design"). Keep the model, "Where BSS falls", "Why: collinearity", "Choosing a design" and the take-home in every length. Saves about 5.5 minutes.

Decided after review rounds 1–2 (author, 2026-10-28)

  • NC example map: keep the published map. The script presents it as a suggested, best-effort allocation for the state's irregular geography and says further restrictions could guarantee that no intervention district borders another.
  • Why spillover into controls: the proposed studies assume a consistent treatment effect, so treated districts gain nothing more from other treated districts, while nearby controls can pick the program up. In Case 2, a trained provider who serves several counties carries it into control counties too.
  • Who BSS beats: framed as downside risk chosen before the trial. Many random draws that keep β identified do better than a checkerboard, but which one can only be known after the fact, and the worst draw on every grid passes the same check (backup "Downside risk").
  • Scale of ρ: stays in backup, with a prepared answer in its notes about the subject-level generating weights and the cluster-level model in the paper.
  • ψ is not the target: the project estimates β; that ψ is not estimable under the checkerboards matters only through β̂ ≈ β − ψ.
  • Refining the NC map: the Recommendation slide now says a refined allocation could also leave a few control districts with no intervention neighbor (author approved rewording, 2026-10-28).
  • Larger grids: the 3×3/3×4 slide shows every allocation (boxes) and each BSS allocation (diamonds), so the spread of random draws is visible.

3. When a program is delivered to whole communities, trials randomize places, and places have neighbors

1 minboth
none
Slide text
A cluster randomized trial (CRT) assigns whole groups, here geographic areas, to intervention or control It is the natural design when a program, policy or supervision practice is delivered to an area rather than to one person Geographic clusters share borders, so what happens in one area can depend on its neighbors Two separate mechanisms create that dependence, spillover and spatial dependence, and both affect …
Notes
When a program is delivered to a whole community, such as a supervision practice in a probation office, we can't randomize individual people, so a cluster randomized trial assigns whole areas to intervention or control. When those clusters are geographic, they have neighbors.
Prelim note
Serves as the prelim's shared motivation for cluster trials of places. Part II builds on it.
Conference note
Cut first for a statistics audience in a 10–15 minute slot (keep one sentence on the next slide).

4. Treatment can spill over into neighboring untreated areas

0.75 minboth
none
Slide text
Bed nets, northern Ghana Child mortality was lower in control villages near villages given insecticide-treated bed nets than in more distant control villages. School deworming, western Kenya Untreated children attending schools near treated schools had fewer worm infections. Spillover is a treatment effect that crosses a cluster boundary A standard CRT analysis assumes a cluster's outcome depends only on its own …
Notes
Two classic trials show what spillover looks like. In northern Ghana, child mortality was lower in control villages near villages that received treated bed nets than in control villages farther away.
Prelim note
Shared motivation; Part II refers back to it rather than repeating the examples.

5. Neighboring outcomes are also correlated for reasons that have nothing to do with treatment

0.75 minboth
none
Slide text
Spatial dependence Nearby areas share demographics, labor markets, service providers and local practice, so their outcomes move together whether or not anyone is treated. It violates the independence that a standard analysis assumes and can understate standard errors Measured by Moran's *I* or Geary's *C*, and modeled through a spatial weights matrix that records who neighbors whom Spillover Caused by the …
Notes
The second mechanism is spatial dependence. Neighboring areas share demographics, labor markets, service providers and local practice, so their outcomes move together whether or not anyone is treated.
Prelim note
Shared motivation; Part II refers back to it.
Conference note
In a 10–15 minute slot, fold into one sentence on "Spillover".

6. Spatial methods mostly adjust after the data are in, and guidance on which clusters to treat is thin

0.75 minboth
none
Slide text
After the trial (analysis) Add a measure of exposure, such as distance to the nearest treated area or the density of treated neighbors Or model space directly in the mean or covariance, as in spatial regression and multiple-membership models Reanalyses show these choices can change the estimated effect and its uncertainty A review of spatial CRT analyses set aside trials that handled space only by design Before …
Notes
Most spatial methods for cluster trials adjust after the data are in, either with an exposure measure such as distance to the nearest treated area or by modeling space directly. On the design side there are restricted randomization, buffer zones and saturation designs, but few studies compare simple allocation rules when spillover and spatial dependence occur together.
Prelim note
Part I's own prior work and gap. Part II adds heterogeneous incidence to it.
Conference note
In a 15–20 minute slot, keep; in a 10–15 minute slot, reduce to the bottom card.

7. Does the allocation chosen before the trial change how well we estimate the effect?

0.75 minboth
none
Slide text
Simple random sampling (SRS) Any balanced allocation of clusters to intervention and control (4 and 5 on the 3×3 grid), chosen at random. The usual default. Block stratified sampling (BSS) A spatially constrained allocation in which no two intervention clusters share an edge, so treated clusters are kept apart in a checkerboard-like pattern. An allocation is the list of which clusters get the intervention We …
Notes
So the question is whether the allocation chosen before the trial, meaning the list of which clusters get the intervention, changes how well we can estimate the effect. Simple random sampling draws any balanced allocation at random, and block stratified sampling keeps treated clusters from touching, in a checkerboard-like pattern.

2. Methods

8. This study defines neighbors as clusters that share an edge

0.5 minboth
Slide text
Rook neighbors share an edge, queen neighbors share an edge or a corner, and higher-order neighbors are neighbors of neighbors Distance-based neighbors lie within a fixed radius We use rook neighbors throughout, and they decide both who can receive spillover and who is spatially correlated
Notes
Everything depends on how we define a neighbor. Rook neighbors share an edge, queen neighbors share an edge or a corner, and you can also define neighbors by distance or as neighbors of neighbors.
Conference note
In a 10–15 minute slot, cut and say "rook neighbors" on the designs slide.

9. Block stratified sampling keeps intervention clusters from sharing an edge

1 minboth
Slide text
SRS may draw any balanced allocation, including ones that put all treated clusters together BSS requires that no two intervention clusters share an edge, and no two controls where the grid allows On the 2×4 and 3×4 grids that leaves only the two checkerboards On the 3×3 grid the arms cannot be balanced, so only intervention clusters must be separated, and 6 allocations qualify; the strict one is shown
Notes
Here are the two designs on the three grids we study, with a block stratified allocation on top and one random allocation below. Simple random sampling can draw any balanced allocation, including ones that put every treated cluster together, like the bottom row.

11. A spatial lag model separates the intervention effect, spillover and spatial dependence

1.25 minboth
none
Slide text
$$ y_i \;=\; \alpha \;+\; \beta\, x_i \;+\; \psi\, z_i \;+\; \rho \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} w_{ij}\, y_j \;+\; \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2) $$ Control Clusters Only $z_i = 1$ if $x_i = 0$ and $x_j = 1$ for some $j \in \mathcal{N}(i)$ Control & Intervention Clusters $z_i = 1$ if $x_j = 1$ for some $j \in \mathcal{N}(i)$ $y_i$ Cluster-level outcome of cluster $i$ $\alpha$ …
Notes
This is the spatial lag model behind every result, and every symbol is defined below. A cluster's outcome is a baseline alpha, plus the intervention effect beta if the cluster is treated, plus the spillover effect psi if it is exposed.

16. With spillover into controls only, an allocation that exposes every control makes exposure the exact opposite of treatment

1.25 minboth
Slide text
Under Control Clusters Only, if every control is exposed then $z_i = 1 - x_i$ for every cluster, $[\mathbf{1}, x, z]$ loses rank, and $\beta$ and $\psi$ cannot be separated. lagsarlm drops $z$, and $\hat\beta$ estimates $\beta - \psi$ At $\rho = 0$ the 2×4 BSS bias is $-\psi$ (-0.50 to -0.80); with spatial dependence the lag term absorbs part of it (-0.35 to -0.72) Control Clusters Only. Every checkerboard and …
Notes
Here is the reason. With spillover into controls only, whenever every control borders an intervention cluster, the spillover indicator is exactly one minus the treatment indicator, so the model can't tell the intervention effect from the spillover effect.

5. Discussion

21. Match the design to the spillover and spatial correlation you expect

1 minboth
none
Slide text
[table] 2×4 values at ψ = 0.5; the direction holds across ψ. For probation districts, which share courts, providers and labor markets, the first column is the realistic one.
Notes
Putting the results together, the design should follow from what investigators expect about spillover and spatial correlation. If spillover flows into controls and neighboring outcomes move together, which is the realistic case for probation districts, block stratified sampling had the lower error and avoided the worst draws.

22. Block stratified sampling is a good design, not the best or the worst, against rolling the dice on one random draw

1 minboth
none
Slide text
Choose the allocation for the spillover you expect, and know what a single random draw can cost Risk, not just the average SRS can win on average, but one trial runs one allocation, and some random draws estimate the effect poorly. The spillover type matters BSS helps most when spillover flows into controls and outcomes are spatially correlated, and most random allocations beat it when spillover reaches both …
Notes
The take-home is that block stratified sampling is a good design, not the best and not the worst, and the comparison that matters is with rolling the dice on a single random draw. Random allocation can win on average, but a trial runs one allocation, and some random draws estimate the effect poorly.
Conference note
Keep in every length.

23. These results come from small regular grids and a simple spillover model

0.5 minboth
none
Slide text
Limitations Treatment and spillover are exactly collinear whenever every control is exposed, which includes every checkerboard Binary rook spillover, with no decay over distance and no added effect from more treated neighbors Small regular grids of equal-area clusters No intra-cluster correlation; results specific to the spatial lag model with the spillover term included Next steps Distance-decaying and additive …
Notes
The most important limitation is the collinearity, which arises whenever every control is exposed. Spillover is binary and limited to rook neighbors, the grids are small and regular, and the model has no intra-cluster correlation and is fitted with the spillover term included.
Prelim note
Keeps the paper reference. Add one closing sentence pointing to Part II (larger grids, heterogeneous incidence, queen neighbors, more designs).

B9. How large is ρ = 0.01?

both
none
Slide text
In the simulation code, outcomes were generated for the subjects with subject-level binary weights, linking each subject to every subject in a rook-neighboring cluster, about 40 to 60 links The model is fitted with the row-normalized version of the same neighbor structure On that fitted scale, $\rho = 0.01$ in the generating process corresponds to roughly $0.01 \times (40\text{ to }60) \approx 0.4$ to $0.6$, and …
Notes
Use when asked "isn't ρ = 0.01 essentially zero?", why adding it changes the error so much, or how the subject-level and cluster-level weights relate. On the scale of the fitted model it is about one half. If asked about the weights, say plainly that outcomes were simulated for subjects within clusters, with a subject-level weights matrix linking each subject to every subject in the neighboring clusters, and the model was fitted to the subjects. Every subject in a cluster shares x, z and neighbors, so the cluster's signal is the subjects' common mean, which is why the paper writes the model at the cluster level with row-normalized weights. The two scales of ρ differ, which this slide shows. Results are reported as published; review/notes/2026-10-28-rho-scale-note.md records a quick check of how the generating weights affect the comparison, which would be the first thing to examine in follow-up work.

both
none
Slide text
Spillover $\psi$ Caused by treatment crossing a boundary. A coefficient on the exposure indicator $z_i$, of direct scientific interest, and zero if no one is treated. Spatial dependence $\rho$ Background correlation from shared conditions, present with or without treatment. A nuisance parameter that must be modeled for valid inference. Both use the same rook neighbors, so they are hard to separate when both are …
Notes
Use when asked "aren't spillover and spatial autocorrelation the same thing?"
